newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine hake stocks ravaged by overfishing.
newsitem.headline: Argentine hake stocks ravaged by overfishing.

text.p: The environmental group Greenpeace said on Wednesday that hake stocks in Argentina have been sharply depleted by overfishing and the government acknowledged it was a problem it would address urgently.
"We admit there's overfishing of hake," said Agriculture, Livestock, Fish and Food Secretary Felipe Sola. "We intend to lower the limit. We are thinking of taking many more measures."
Sola spoke to Reuters after Greenpeace, in a protest in the city centre, said hake stocks have shrunk 25 percent in less than 10 years and faced "irreversible collapse".

"There are too many ships catching too few fish. Selective fishing methods are not respected and records stating the amount and species of fish caught are forged," Greenpeace activist Emiliano Ezcurra told reporters at the protest where passers-by were offered hake samples to eat.
Hake is Argentina's main fishing export, bringing in a third, or $300 million, of total fishing revenues in 1996. Total exports soared to $1 billion last year from $220 million in 1986.

Citing statistics from Argentina's National Fishing Investigation and Development Institute (INIDEP), Greenpeace said fishermen now invest twice as much time catching the same amount of hake as five years ago.
And while INIDEP biologists have recommended a limit of 360,000 tonnes, the government set a higher ceiling of 395,000.
"The level should be decided by INIDEP," Sola said, adding that this will be the top priority of the next fishing undersecretary. The last one resigned 10 days ago for health reasons.
Through illegal fishing and bad practices, such as using nets to catch prawns which also kill hake, a total 600,000 specimens die each year, Greenpeace said.
For every tonne of prawns caught, 18 tonnes of hake are killed and discarded -- a practice which could be stopped if the right nets became mandatory.

"These days it takes a lot longer to catch hake, the fish we get are smaller and we have to go to look for them much further south," veteran fisherman Enrique Martinez del Pezzo said at a Greenpeace protest.

"The average weight of each fish is one kilo. It used to be two, or two and a half. And only five years ago, you would throw in your net, drag it along for three or four hours and pull up 35 or 40 tonnes of hake. Now if you get 20 tonnes you can't complain."
